newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI says EU debt, deficit levels unsatisfactory.
newsitem.headline: EMI says EU debt, deficit levels unsatisfactory.

text.p: European Monetary Institute (EMI) President Alexandre Lamfalussy said on Tuesday that convergence of debt and deficit levels among many European Union countries remained far from satisfactory.

In the EMI's annual report, Lamfalussy said that debt consolidation efforts were relying too much on revenue rather than spending cuts and warned that one-off measures or accounting tricks would not achieve sustainable convergence.
Laxity in this regard may reduce confidence in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) project and "may negatively affect financial markets," the EMI report warned.

Lamfalussy said that clear progress had been made towards convergence of inflation and bond yields, other key issues for preparing for the planned euro launch in 1999, and exchange rate stability had been broadly maintained.
"However on the fiscal side, the situation remains far from satisfactory in many countries," Lamfalussy wrote in a foreword to the report.
"Despite efforts made at consolidation, which have contributed to a fall in actual deficits, the latter still overshoot the reference values laid down in the Treaty in most countries."
Lamfalussy noted that debt ratios had continued to rise in the aggregate, despite favourable trends in some member states.
"In my view, the composition of consolidation continues to rely excessively on high revenue ratios and less than is desirable on expenditure cuts," he said.
"Furthermore sustainable convergence cannot be achieved by one-off and accounting measures."

In the report itself, the EMI stressed that "more and durable progress" was needed to ensure sustainable fiscal positions in the EU and warned that laxity in this regard could have a negative effect on financial markets.

The Maastricht Treaty calls for national debts to total no more than 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- or to show significant progress in falling toward this level -- and for budget deficits to be three percent or less barring exceptional circumstances.
Further progress on achieving these goals "will also contribute to sustaining exchange rate stability and the convergence of bond yields," the EMI said.
On the other hand, "setbacks in the consolidation of public finances or other factors that may reduce confidence in the EMU process may negatively affect financial markets."
